lead: A wing spar cap bends under moment. One section property, the second moment of area I, gives both the stress at every point and the curved shape. For a moment about a principal axis: σ = M y / I and 1/R = M/EI. Poisson contraction makes the cross-section curl the other way: anticlastic bending. Spar, stringer and frame sizing starts here.
prereq: You need the second moment of area, the parallel-axis theorem, and the wing bending moment diagram from Unit 1.

blocks.text: Bending is symmetrical when the moment acts about a principal axis and the section is symmetric about the plane of bending. Five assumptions:

items: Plane sections stay plane and normal to the bent axis.
Deflections are small, so curvature 1/R ≈ d²v/dx².
The material is linear elastic, with equal E in tension and compression.
The moment acts about a principal axis; no axial force acts.
The wall is thin enough for uniform stress across its thickness (see 4.4).
A plane section rotates as a plane. The fibre at distance y from the neutral axis changes length by y/R, so strain is ε = y/R.
Hooke's law gives σ = E ε = E y / R.
No axial force acts: ∫σ dA = (E/R) ∫y dA = 0. The first moment ∫y dA vanishes only about the centroid, so the neutral axis passes through the centroid.
Internal moment equals stress times lever arm: M = ∫σ y dA = (E/R) ∫y² dA = E I / R, where I = ∫y² dA about the neutral axis.
Eliminate R between steps 2 and 4 of this list: σ = M y / I.

blocks.text: σ = M y / I,   1/R = M / EI,   Z = I / y_max
blocks.where: σ is direct stress (Pa or N/mm²) at distance y from the neutral axis; M is bending moment about that axis (N·m); y is distance from the centroidal neutral axis (m), positive towards tension; I is second moment of area about that axis (m⁴); E is Young's modulus (Pa); R is radius of curvature of the beam axis (m); Z is elastic section modulus (m³); y_max is distance to the outermost fibre (m).

blocks.text: Stress grows linearly with y; curvature is fixed by M/EI. The section modulus gives σ_max = M/Z. A rectangular section twice as deep has eight times I but only twice y_max, so σ_max falls four times. This is why spars are deep and skins thin.

sections.h3: Sign convention, stress diagram and section modulus

blocks.text: Take sagging as positive. A simply supported beam under downward load sags: top fibres shorten, bottom fibres stretch. Measure y positive downwards, towards tension. Then σ = +M y / I gives tension below the axis and compression above it. A hogging moment is negative and every sign flips.

items: Stress is zero at the centroidal axis.
Stress varies linearly through the depth, with slope M/I.
Stress is largest at the outer fibre, y = y_max.
For a section symmetric about the axis, top and bottom stresses are equal and opposite.

blocks.text: A section not symmetric about its neutral axis, like a T-section or a wing box with a wide top skin, has different distances to top and bottom fibres and so two section moduli, Z_top = I/y_top and Z_bottom = I/y_bottom. Yielding is governed by the larger distance (the smaller Z), whichever face it is on; the compression face governs skin buckling (see Unit 6). In the example below, I = 8.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and y_max = 0.10 m, so Z = 8.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³.

A stretched fibre contracts sideways by ν ε, where ν is Poisson's ratio: about 0.33 for aluminium alloy, 0.3 for steel. A compressed fibre expands sideways. The transverse strain itself cannot be avoided; only the curl it produces can be restrained.

In a sagging beam the bottom fibre at y = +d/2 has longitudinal strain +y/R, so transverse strain is −ν y/R and it narrows. The top fibre at y = −d/2 widens by +ν y/R. Width change is proportional to y, so the cross-section curls in its own plane.
1/R′ = ν / R,   so   R′ = R / ν
blocks.where: R′ is transverse (anticlastic) radius of curvature of the cross-section (m); R is longitudinal radius of curvature of the beam axis (m); ν is Poisson's ratio, dimensionless.

blocks.text: R′ is about three times R for aluminium, so the curl is visible: bend a rubber eraser and its end face stops being rectangular. The bar becomes a saddle, curving one way along its length and the opposite way across its width.

The curl is free only on a narrow strip. In a wing box, flanges, stringers, ribs and continuous skin hold the section almost flat. Sideways movement is restrained, and a transverse stress σ_t = −ν σ appears in the skin instead. The panel then works biaxially; this matters for fatigue and compression-skin buckling. Free curl survives near edges: cut-outs, free flanges, holes. Thus σ = M y / I serves both cases; deformation and transverse stress differ: the stiffened box works biaxially, the plain strip curls freely.

figure.caption: From moment to stress and transverse curl. Example values: at y = 0.10 m, σ = 235.3 MPa; free anticlastic radius R′ = 90.15 m.

spec.title: From moment to stress and back-curvature
spec.aria: A top-down chain from applied moment to beam curvature, strain, direct stress, and transverse anticlastic curvature from Poisson contraction.

examples.question: An aluminium alloy beam has E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, I = 8.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and depth 200 mm. A moment M = 20 kN·m acts about the horizontal centroidal axis. Find (a) maximum direct stress, (b) beam-axis radius, (c) free anticlastic radius.
steps: Neutral axis is centroidal at mid-depth: y_max = 200/2 = 100 mm = 0.10 m.
Use SI: M = 2.0 × 10⁴ N·m, E = 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa.
(a) σ_max = M y_max / I = (2.0 × 10⁴ × 0.10)/(8.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.35 × 10⁸ Pa = 235.3 MPa, tension on the sagging side.
Check by section modulus: Z = I/y_max = 8.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³; σ_max = M/Z = 235.3 MPa.
(c) R′ = R/ν = 29.75/0.33 = 90.15 m, about three times R.

traps: Measuring y from an outer face, flange or skin instead of the centroidal neutral axis.
Using σ = M y / I when the moment is not about a principal axis; see 4.2.
Mixing units: M in kN·m with I in m⁴ and E in GPa. Convert first.
Writing R′ = νR instead of R/ν. R′ is larger than R.
Using one y_max for an asymmetric section; it has two section moduli.

quiz.q: State the assumptions of simple bending theory for a thin-walled beam.
quiz.a: Plane sections stay plane and normal to the axis; small deflections; linear elastic material with equal E in tension and compression; moment about a principal axis; no axial load; thin wall gives uniform stress across thickness.

quiz.q: Define elastic section modulus and give its unit.
quiz.a: Z = I/y_max, where I is second moment of area about the centroidal neutral axis and y_max is distance to the outermost fibre. Unit: m³ or mm³. σ_max = M/Z.

quiz.q: Why does the neutral axis pass through the centroid?
quiz.a: No axial force acts, so ∫σ dA = 0. With σ = E y/R this needs ∫y dA = 0. A zero first moment defines the centroid. Any parallel axis gives a net axial force.

quiz.q: A beam has I = 12 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ and y_max = 150 mm. Find maximum stress for M = 30 kN·m.
An aluminium strip (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.30, thickness 2 mm) bends to R = 20 m. Find anticlastic radius and transverse strain at the outer fibre.
quiz.a: R′ = R/ν = 20/0.30 = 66.7 m. At y = 1 mm, longitudinal strain = y/R = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵, transverse strain = −ν y/R = −1.5 × 10⁻⁵; that face narrows.

quiz.q: A wing box and a plain strip of the same material bend to the same radius. Why is anticlastic curl visible in the strip but not the box?
quiz.a: On the free strip, side faces move freely, so Poisson strain varies through the depth and the section curls at R′ = R/ν. In the box, flanges, stringers, ribs and skin restrain sideways movement. The section stays nearly flat and Poisson strain appears as transverse stress −νσ in the skin. That biaxial stress affects fatigue and compression buckling, not shape.

quiz.q: Two beams have the same I, but one is 100 mm deep and the other 300 mm deep. Which has higher maximum bending stress for the same moment, and why?
quiz.a: The 300 mm beam, because σ_max = M y_max/I and its y_max is 150 mm against 50 mm. With the same I, outer-fibre stress is three times larger; deep sections win only when I also grows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Anticlastic bending appears as shape loss in thin panels and extra transverse stress near bonded repairs and cut-outs. Orthotropic composites have direction-dependent Poisson effects, so laminate lay-up can cancel curvature. Finite element models capture this in 3D. Search next for plate bending, cylindrical bending and Saint-Venant edge zones.
